headline: Tsukuru is first attested in the Kojiki of 712 CE, ultimately from Proto-Japonic *tukoru.

sources.quote: From Old Japanese. First attested in the Kojiki of 712 CE. Ultimately from Proto-Japonic *tukoru.

headline: Ichi is from Middle Chinese 一 (ʔiɪt̚), and went itɨ → it͡sɨ → it͡ɕɨ on the way.

sources.quote: /itɨ/ → /it͡sɨ/ → /it͡ɕɨ/
From Middle Chinese 一 (ʔiɪt̚).
Compare modern Hokkien 一 (it).

examples.en: I found a dollar in the street.
One word is enough for a wise man.

headline: Shokudō was jikidō, a refectory in a Buddhist temple, before the Meiji period's kan'on reading of 食.

sources.quote: /d͡ʑikidoː/ → /ɕokudoː/

Shift from older reading jikidō (“refectory in a Buddhist temple”). In the Meiji period, the pronunciation shifted to using the kan'on reading of shoku for 食 as the sense expanded to indicate dining facilities in a dormitory, and from there, to any larger room for serving or selling food to multiple people.
First attested in 1903.

examples.ja: 食堂は何時にあきますか。
examples.en: What time does the dining room open?

headline: Jimusho is, by surface analysis, 事務 (jimu) plus 所 (-sho).

sources.quote: By surface analysis, 事務(じむ) (jimu) + 所(しょ) (-sho).

pos: nouns which may take the genitive case particle 'no'
headline: Tsugi is a nominalization of the stem of the verb 次ぐ (tsugu, “to follow, to be next; to connect”).

sources.quote: Nominalization of the 連用形 (ren'yōkei, “continuative or stem form”) of Old Japanese-derived verb 次ぐ (tsugu, “to be in a sequence; to follow, to continue from something, to be next; to connect, to join”).

headline: Katachi is 形 (kata, “shape, form”) plus ち (-chi), but the chi element's derivation is unclear.

sources.quote: From Old Japanese. First attested in the Nihon Shoki of 720 CE.
Probably related to 堅い / 硬い / 固い (katai, “hard”).
Compound of 形 (kata, “shape, form”) + ち (-chi), but the derivation of the chi element is unclear.

examples.en: An apple is round in shape.

headline: Kuruma is attested in phonetic spelling as 久流末 (kuruma), and may originally have meant “wheel”.

sources.quote: From Old Japanese. Appears in the Man'yōshū completed some time after 759 CE, with the ideographic spelling 車. Also attested in the 正倉院文書 (Shōsō-in Bunsho) set of documents dated to the Nara period, appearing in the phonetic (man'yōgana) spelling of 久流末 (kuruma).

Assuming an initial meaning of wheel, may be a compound of くる (kuru, related to spinning or rotating, as in 繰る (kuru, “to spin (as in thread)”), 枢 (kuru, “hinge”), くるくる (kurukuru, “spinningly, round and round”), 転めく (kurumeku, “to spin round and round, to rotate; to be dizzy”)) + ま (ma, a suffix added to various parts of speech to form an indeclinable word indicating state).

headline: Chikatetsu is a clipping of 地下鉄道 (chika tetsudō, “underground railway”).

sources.quote: Clipping of 地(ち)下(か)鉄(てつ)道(どう) (chika tetsudō, “underground railway”), itself 地下(ちか) (chika, “underground”) + 鉄道(てつどう) (tetsudō, “railway”).

examples.ja: 地下鉄は地面の下を走る。

headline: Kippu is 切る (kiru, “cut”) plus 符 (fu, “tally split in half used for identification”).

sources.quote: From 切(き)る (kiru, “cut, slice, carve”) + 符(ふ) (fu, “tally split in half used for identification”).

examples.en: The ticket holds good for three days.

headline: Daigakusei is 大学 (daigaku, “university”) plus 生 (-sei, “student; pupil”).

sources.quote: 大(だい)学(がく) (daigaku, “university”) + 生(せい) (-sei, “student; pupil”).

headline: Kanji is a Middle Chinese compound, literally “Han Chinese + character”.

sources.quote: From Middle Chinese compound 漢字 (MC xanH dziH, literally “Han Chinese + character”). Compare modern Mandarin 漢字／汉字 (hànzì), Hokkien 漢字 /汉字 (hàn-jī / hàn-lī).

examples.ja: 漢字は読むのが難しい。
彼は漢字が全く書けない。

headline: Kinō went kinopu → kinoɸu → kinowu → kinou → kinoː, and its initial ki is unclear.

sources.quote: /ki no pu/ → /kinoɸu/ → */kinowu/ → /kinou/ → /kinoː/
From Old Japanese, ultimately from Proto-Japonic *kinəpu.

The initial ki is unclear, but is likely the same ki element that appears in other words pertaining to the past. This may be related to the now-obsolete auxiliary verb き (ki) indicating the recollective past -- see けり (keri). The middle no appears to be the regular genitive particle の (no). The final pu is an apophonic form of 日 (hi, “day”), also found in 今日 (kepu→kyō, “today”).

Martin suggests that the initial ki might also be related to Old Japanese 來 (ku, “to come”), modern 来る (kuru), presumably via the 連用形 (ren'yōkei, “continuative or stem form”) of ki. However, this is problematic both semantically, as "the coming day" would presumably refer to tomorrow rather than yesterday; and grammatically, as a verb modifying a noun would be expected to conjugate into the regular attributive form (for 來 (ku) that would be kuru), rather than into the continuative form that then necessitates a particle.
The kanji are orthographic borrowing from Chinese 昨日 (zuórì).

headline: Mon is from Middle Chinese 門 (MC mwon).

sources.quote: From Middle Chinese 門 (MC mwon).

examples.en: The tongue wounds more than a lance.

headline: Atsui for weather and 熱い for objects share one source: Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *atu.

sources.quote: From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *atu.
Cognate with 熱(あつ)い (atsui, “hot (of an object)”).

headline: Ireru developed from the classical lower bigrade verb 入る, meaning to put something into something.

sources.quote: Regular development of classical 下(しも)二(に)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo nidan katsuyō, “lower bigrade conjugation”) verb 入(い)る (iru, “to put something into something else”, transitive).
Development

Natural progression from Old and Classical Japanese 下(しも)二(に)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo nidan katsuyō, “lower bigrade conjugation”) verbs ending in -u to modern Japanese 下(しも)一(いち)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo ichidan katsuyō, “lower monograde conjugation”) verbs ending in -eru. For the Old / Classical form, see the 入る entry.
Active form of 入(い)る (iru, “to enter, to go into something”, intransitive) and its alternative form 要(い)る (iru, “to need, to require”).

examples.en: Run hot water into the bath.

headline: Yureru comes from the lower bigrade intransitive classical verb 揺る (yuru).

sources.quote: Derived via regular historical processes from the 下二段活用 (shimo nidan katsuyō, “lower bigrade conjugation”) intransitive form of classical Japanese verb 揺る (yuru), itself from Old Japanese.
Development

Natural progression from Old and Classical Japanese 下(しも)二(に)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo nidan katsuyō, “lower bigrade conjugation”) verbs ending in -u to modern Japanese 下(しも)一(いち)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo ichidan katsuyō, “lower monograde conjugation”) verbs ending in -eru. For the Old / Classical form, see the 揺る entry.

examples.en: The buildings shook in the earthquake.

headline: Iku has a hidden twin: yuku, thanks to an old habit of inserting a y glide before vowels.

sources.quote: From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *iku. Cognate with Okinawan 行(い)ちゅん (ichun), Miyako 行きぃ (iksï).

The original Proto‐Japonic root was vowel‐initial, as evidenced by the Ryukyuan cognates. In Old Japanese, a prothetic glide /j/ was often inserted before certain vowel‐initial words to ease pronunciation. This phonological innovation created the variant form 行(ゆ)く (yuku), paralleling the i‐ ~ yu‐ alternation seen in the archaic noun 夢 (ime₂) versus modern 夢(ゆめ) (yume).

Because the innovative yuku form was heavily utilized in foundational classical literature, such as the Man’yōshū, it became fossilized as the high‐prestige, conservative literary standard. Meanwhile, the direct descendant iku persisted as the common spoken vernacular and was ultimately adopted as the standard for modern spoken Japanese.

headline: Shinsetsu is literally “blood relative + close”, a Middle Chinese compound.

sources.quote: From Middle Chinese compound 親切 /亲切 (tshin tshet, literally “blood relative + close”).

headline: Ushiro may be from us- (“lost; gone”) plus a locative suffix, but the ultimate derivation is unknown.

sources.quote: From Old Japanese. Appears in the Kojiki of 712 CE. Also cited to a portion of the Shoku Nihongi dated to 781, with the phonetic spelling 宇志呂 (usiro₂). In turn, from Proto-Japonic *osirə. Cognate with Hachijō おしろ (oshiro).

Ultimate derivation unknown. Might be from stem us- ("lost; gone, out of sight", as in 失う (ushinau, “to lose”), older verb 失す (usu, “to lose; to go away”)) + locative suffix -ro₂ indicating an interior (as in 所 (tokoro, “place”), 空ろ・虚ろ (utsuro, “emptiness, a hollow”), 洞・空・虚 (uro, “a hollow space in something”), 室 (muro, “room; cave”), possibly 心 (kokoro, “heart”)). The earliest sense of "somewhere out of sight" also suggests a connection with stem us-.

pos: nouns which may take the genitive case particle 'no'
headline: Tonari may be 外 (to1, “outside, other”) plus nari, but the source gives two analyses of the second part.

sources.quote: ⟨to₁nari⟩ → */tʷonari/ → /tonari/
From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *tonari.

Analyzable as a compound of Old Japanese 外 (to₁, “outside, other”) + nari, possibly the nominalization of verb なる (naru, “to become”), or a contraction of に (ni, locative particle) + あり (ari, copular "to be" verb, predicative and nominal form).

examples.en: The devil lurks behind the cross.
He seated himself next to me.

headline: Maitsuki is “every + month” and is first attested in roughly 1215.

sources.quote: Compound of 毎 (mai, “every, each”) + 月 (getsu, “month; moon”).
First attested in roughly 1215.

headline: Isogashii is derived from the verb 急ぐ (isogu, “to hurry”), first attested in a text from 850.

sources.quote: Derived from verb 急ぐ (isogu, “to hurry, to rush, to hasten”).
First attested in a text from 850.
By one analysis, this is the verb's 未然形 (mizenkei, “incomplete or irrealis form”) 急が (isoga) plus the adjectivizing suffix しい (-shii, “having that kind of quality”, classical terminal form -shi).

Alternatively, may be derived from the causative. The classical terminal form of the adjective is identical to the classical continuative or infinitive form of the causative verb, which was used in certain constructions to conclude sentences.
* 急ぐ (isogu, “to rush, to hurry”) → 急がす (isogasu, “to cause to rush, to cause to hurry”) → 急がし (isogashi, “having the quality of causing one to rush or hurry”)

headline: Hyaku is borrowed from Middle Chinese 百 (MC paek, literally “hundred”).

sources.quote: Borrowed from Middle Chinese 百 (MC paek, literally “hundred”).

headline: Hikōki is first attested in 1908, and is 飛行 (hikō, “flying, flight”) plus 機 (-ki, “machine”), a calque of English flying machine.

sources.quote: First attested in 1908, cited from the 万朝報 (Yorozu Chōho) serial in its October 3 issue.
From 飛行(ひこう) (hikō, “flying, flight”) + 機(き) (-ki, “machine”), a calque of English flying machine.

meaning: I (used by men towards those of equal or lower status)
headline: Boku shifted from the kun'yomi of shimobe or yatsugare to the on'yomi, and became prevalent around the Meiji period.

sources.quote: Shift in reading from the kun'yomi of shimobe or yatsugare to use the on'yomi of boku instead, first attested in kundoku contexts from the mid-to-late 1700s and becoming prevalent from around the Meiji period.

meaning: to enter, to contain, to hold
headline: Hairu is from older 這ひ入る (fafiiru): a compound of 這ひ (fafi, from 這ふ, “to crawl”) plus 入る (iru, “to enter”).

sources.quote: From older 這(は)ひ入(い)る (fafiiru, modern pronunciation 這(は)い入(い)る (haiiru)), itself a compound of 這(は)ひ (fafi, modern pronunciation 這(は)い (hai), 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 這(は)ふ (fafu, “to crawl”, modern pronunciation 這(は)う (hau))) + 入(い)る (iru, “to enter, to go in”).
* /faɸiiru/ → /fawiiru/ → /faiiru/ → /fairu/ → /hairu/
This shortened hairu form is first attested from the early 1200s.

headline: Kanashii historically also meant “dear; beloved; lovely”, in addition to “sad”.

sources.quote: ⟨kanasiki₁⟩ → /kanasiki/ → /kanaɕiː/
From Old Japanese 悲し (kanasi-, “emotionally overwhelming: dear, beloved, sad”), ultimately from Proto-Japonic *kanasi- (“beloved, dear”). First attested in the Kojiki of 712 CE.

Historically also meant "dear; beloved; lovely", in addition to "sad". The former senses were later taken over by other adjectives such as 愛らしい (airashii), 愛しい (itoshii), and 可愛い (kawaii). See also the Ryukyuan cognates such as Miyako かなすぃ゚ (kanasï) and Okinawan かなさん (kanasan, “beloved, lovely, cute”), which do not mean "sad".
Considering the original sense of "emotionally overwhelming", might be cognate with 兼ねる (kaneru, “to group together; to be concerned about something”), from the semantic overlap with grief.

headline: Nuru is possibly related to 濡れる (nureru, “to get wet”).

sources.quote: From Old Japanese. Possibly related to 濡(ぬ)れる (nureru, “to get wet”).

examples.en: We're going to paint the wall.

headline: Higashi was hingashi: /ɸiŋɡaɕi/ → /ɸiɡaɕi/ → /hiɡaɕi/.

sources.quote: /ɸiŋɡaɕi/ → /ɸiɡaɕi/ → /hiɡaɕi/
Sound shift from hingashi (see Etymology 2 below).
Now the standard word for east.

examples.en: The moon rises in the east.

examples.ja: 風は東から吹いている。
examples.en: The wind is blowing from the east.

meaning: to cross over, to go across
headline: Wataru is Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *wataru.

sources.quote: From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *wataru.
